title: A giraffe's neck has the same number of bones as yours: seven
body: Almost all mammals have exactly seven neck vertebrae, and the giraffe, with a neck up to 2.4 m long, is no exception. Instead of adding extra bones, evolution made each one enormous: every giraffe neck vertebra is [over 28 cm long](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giraffe). They get that big because the embryo keeps growing these bones for longer, a shift in developmental timing called **heterochrony**. The only mammals known to break the rule of seven are manatees and sloths.

cover.alt: A giraffe standing in tall golden grass, looking straight at the camera, with wooded hills behind it

slides.heading: Seven neck vertebrae, or not?
slides.explanation: Manatees have six and three-toed sloths have nine. Two-toed sloths, with five or six, are the third known exception.

slides.heading: Neck vertebrae in four mammals
slides.note: Two-toed sloths have five or six; nearly every other mammal has seven

slides.alt: A mounted giraffe skeleton in a museum, its long neck made of a short row of very long vertebrae
slides.caption: A giraffe skeleton in the National Museum of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Count the neck bones between the skull and the shoulders.

left.label: Okapi
left.text: The giraffe's closest living relative. Its neck vertebrae make up 27 to 33% of the spine's length, typical of large hoofed mammals.

right.label: Giraffe
right.text: Neck vertebrae make up about 52 to 54% of the spine, with the same seven bones.

slides.heading: Stretched, not added
slides.text: Both animals start with the same mammal blueprint of seven neck bones. In the giraffe embryo those bones simply keep growing for longer, so the difference lies in timing, not in how many bones there are.

slides.question: How did the giraffe end up with such a long neck?
options: Its ribs extend up the neck
Its skull sits on a long tendon
slides.explanation: It kept the mammal standard of seven neck vertebrae and lengthened each one, to over 28 cm.
